human_tolerance.notes: 'The northern flicker may be observed in open habitats near trees, including woodlands, edges, yards, and parks.' It excavates cavities in trees, may use posts and birdhouses where suitably sized, and 'can create cavities inside homes, especially homes of stucco or weak wooden siding', but is 'sometimes driven away from its nesting site by other cavity nesters like the common starling'. flight_distance_m is judgement, not a sourced number.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: 'The northern flicker commonly breeds during the months of February to July, depending upon the temperature of the area.' One to two clutches per season, typically six to eight pure white glossy eggs, the second-largest of any North American woodpecker; incubation by both sexes for about 11 to 12 days; young fledge about 25 to 28 days after hatching.

phases.name: nesting
phases.note: One to two weeks for a mated pair to build the nest. Both sexes excavate a cavity about 33-41 cm deep with an entrance roughly 5-10 cm wide, often facing east to south-east, lined only with a bed of wood chips; occasionally an old kingfisher or sand martin burrow is used.

phases.name: territorial
phases.note: Males locate females by head bobbing and their personal mating call 'woikawoikawoika'; used toward a male the same call is a territorial signal, reinforced by head swinging, bill-pointing and drumming on wood or metal with the wings spread and the tail flashed.

phases.name: dispersal
phases.note: 'Those that do migrate tend to begin their spring migration towards the beginning of April and make their return between September and October.' Some southern populations are completely non-migratory.

vocalizations.description: 'This bird's call is a sustained laugh, ki ki ki ki.' The male's mating call toward a female is described as 'woikawoikawoika', a call that 'drums and rattles' and rises into a loud noise; used toward another male the same call is a territorial signal.

'One may also hear a constant knocking as they often drum on trees or even metal objects to declare territory... the purpose is to make as loud a noise as possible, so woodpeckers sometimes drum on metal objects.' While drumming the bird spreads its wings and flashes its colourful tail underside.

external.note: GBIF usage key, authorship and order from the GBIF Backbone Taxonomy; the iNaturalist taxa API matched taxon 18236 to 'Northern Flicker'; ITIS TSN and NCBI taxon id from Wikidata (P815, P685). Wikidata P2050 also carries a wingspan of 49.4 cm (48.1-50.7 cm), consistent with the range quoted from Wikipedia.

common_names.note: Wikipedia notes 'Over 100 common names for the northern flicker are known', several derived from attempts to imitate its calls; the standard English name and the French and Spanish names used here are the conventional ones.

conservation.note: Wikidata P141 = least concern. The Wikipedia article carries no conservation section, so the CC0 Wikidata statement is the authority here.

range.note: 'It is native to most of North America, parts of Central America, Cuba, and the Cayman Islands'; 'The northern flicker may be observed in open habitats near trees, including woodlands, edges, yards, and parks. In the western United States, one can find it in mountain forests all the way up to the tree line'; it 'breeds during the months of February to July'. The state list is an approximation covering the contiguous United States from that description and is not exhaustive; Central America is named only as 'parts of Central America' in the source, so no Central American country is itemised. No elevation range is given in the source, so elevation_m is omitted.

traits.note: Covers the structural traits (body plan, limb count, thermoregulation, skin, flight, respiration, metamorphosis, perching) and locomotion modes: the species 'frequently feed[s] on the ground' by probing, climbs tree trunks to excavate and roost, and flies in the characteristic undulating woodpecker flight ('a quick succession of flaps followed by a pause'). Individual numeric and behavioural traits below carry their own entries.

traits.nest_type.note: 'The northern flicker generally nests in holes in trees like other woodpeckers... Both sexes help with the nest excavation. The entrance hole is about 8 cm in diameter, and the cavity is 33-41 cm deep.'

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg (~0.13 kg); the validator's size-class bands place this in the Small band.

traits.mass_kg.note: Midpoint of the stated 86-167 g range, 126.5 g, rounded to 0.127 kg.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: Stated range 86-167 g. The source notes the largest-bodied specimens come from the northern range (Alaska and Labrador) and the smallest from Grand Cayman.

traits.wingspan_m.note: Midpoint of the stated 42-54 cm, as a direct conversion of the sourced wingspan.

traits.lifespan_y.note: Derived, and an explicit gap. The source gives record ages rather than a typical lifespan: 'The oldest yet known "yellow-shafted" northern flicker lived to be at least 9 years 2 months old', and the red-shafted record is 8 years 9 months. A 2006 six-year capture-mark-recapture study found only one to two birds in every 300 adults reached 7 years or more, and a mortality model predicted a 0.6% 7-year survival rate, so the typical wild lifespan is shorter than any of these figures. 4.6 years is half the 9.2-year record, which is the usual rough relationship between a record longevity and a typical one in a small passerine; the value is an order-of-magnitude estimate, not a measurement.

traits.diet.note: Diet section: 'Although they eat fruits, berries, seeds, and nuts, their primary food is insects. Ants alone can make up 45% of their diet', plus flies, butterflies, moths, beetles and snails, and 'berries and seeds, especially in winter'. The insect share is set near the sourced 45% floor and rounded up because the figure is a single-ant figure rather than a whole-insect one; the plant shares are judgement.

traits.social.note: 'During the breeding season, both mates stay together. After the season, they do not stay together', and both sexes incubate the eggs and feed the young.

traits.activity_pattern.note: Judgement: the source describes daytime ground foraging, courtship calls and territorial drumming, and a nocturnal cavity roost, without labelling the pattern.

traits.defense.note: Judgement: the species has strong territorial signals against other flickers (head swinging, bill-pointing, drumming) but no sourced predator defence, and the shared perching-songbird program's default response to a close threat is to move away, so Flee was authored.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: it feeds openly in yards and parks and excavates in buildings, but 'is sometimes driven away from its nesting site by other cavity nesters' and it needs undisturbed nest sites; a middling value was authored.

habitat.note: Covers shelter_tag and habitat.resources. Invertebrate, fruit, berry and seed tags come from the Diet section; cavity from the nest excavation; perch from drumming, roosting and courtship on trees. Weights are judgement, not separately sourced percentages.

habitat.use.note: 'flickers are the only woodpeckers that frequently feed on the ground', probing with the beak and sometimes catching insects in flight, while nesting and roosting in tree cavities and foraging on fruit and seeds in trees and shrubs.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Habitat and Reproduction sections: observed 'in open habitats near trees, including woodlands, edges, yards, and parks'; 'may also use posts and birdhouses if sized and situated appropriately'; 'They can create cavities inside homes, especially homes of stucco or weak wooden siding'; but 'sometimes driven away from its nesting site by other cavity nesters like the common starling'. flight_distance_m is judgement, not a sourced number.

seasonal.strategy.note: 'Northern flickers are partial migrants, some southern populations being completely non-migratory', so PartialMigration was used rather than Migration.

seasonal.phases.note: Breeding February to July with one to two clutches and the quoted clutch, incubation and fledging figures; nest excavation taking one to two weeks; courtship and territorial behaviour through the breeding season; and a September-October return migration with spring movement from early April. The source gives months rather than days, so day-of-month boundaries are judgement. The breeding phase is tagged US-CO because the locale that prompted this record is in Colorado; the source's dates are continental.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Egg (six to eight pure white, smooth, high-gloss eggs, the second-largest of any North American woodpecker), altricial juvenile (fledged about 25-28 days after hatching; 'juvenile northern flickers are often helpless against predators who enter the nest') and adult. No sourced juvenile-plumage duration was found, so duration_days is unset and the juvenile scale is judgement.

vocalizations.wheeko.note: Call and flight and Reproduction sections: 'This bird's call is a sustained laugh, ki ki ki ki'; 'The common sounds a male makes towards a female is woikawoikawoika... If the call is used towards a male, it is a territorial sign', and 'The call type is a chirp that drums and rattles'. It fills both the song and alarm slots because the source presents one call serving both functions.

vocalizations.drumming.note: Call and flight section: 'One may also hear a constant knocking as they often drum on trees or even metal objects to declare territory.' Cooldown is judgement.

look.note: Description section: 'Adults are brown with black bars on the back and wings... A necklace-like black patch occupies the upper breast, while the lower breast and belly are beige with black spots. Males can be identified by a black (in the eastern part of the species' range) or red (in the western part) mustachial stripe at the base of the beak... The tail is dark on top, transitioning to a white rump which is conspicuous in flight.' Colorado birds are red-shafted, so the accent colour carries the red-shafted tail and undertail flash; the barred back and wings are placed on the wing-outer and body slots; proportions are authored judgement.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared perching-songbird program: food_tag is the insect share the program uses for ground foraging, which is this species' defining habit; flee_m and wariness are middling for a bird that feeds in open yards; nest_m1/nest_m2 span the stated February-July breeding season.
